Key Research Thinking Patterns: Developmental Comparative Analysis: Investigating how social constructs and peer status attributes evolve across life stages by contrasting self-report and observational data from distinct developmental cohorts. (e.g., Comparing open-ended descriptions of peer popularity in high school versus college to identify a shift from appearance-based to prosocial-based status metrics.)

Multidisciplinary Forensic Integration: Combining qualitative social science inquiry with quantitative engineering assessments to evaluate complex real-world disaster outcomes and human behavior. (e.g., Integrating semistructured survivor interviews with forensic structural engineering and parametric tornado wind field modeling to assess residential survivability and sheltering efficacy.)

Experimental Causal Inference: Utilizing controlled experimental designs and priming paradigms to isolate specific psychological mechanisms driving social perceptions and behaviors. (e.g., Employing priming paradigms and vignette methodologies to experimentally test the causal link between gender prototypicality and perceived peer popularity, power, and attractiveness.)

Hierarchical Multivariate Modeling: Applying advanced statistical techniques to disentangle the unique and interactive contributions of multiple social support sources to psychological outcomes. (e.g., Using hierarchical regression and moderation analysis to determine the distinct roles of family, offline friend, and online friend support in the psychological adjustment of transgender and nonbinary young adults.)
Summary Description: Lara Mayeux is a developmental and social psychologist at the University of Oklahoma specializing in adolescent peer relations, gender dynamics, and disaster risk reduction. Her research employs a dual-track methodological approach: in social psychology, she utilizes experimental designs, priming paradigms, and hierarchical regression to examine how gender typicality and developmental transitions influence peer status, popularity, and social integration. In disaster science, she integrates forensic structural engineering, wind field modeling, and qualitative survivor interviews to assess residential tornado vulnerability and sheltering strategies. Her work bridges psychological adjustment in LGBTQ+ youth with physical safety in extreme weather events, leveraging tools like the Gender Minority Stress and Resilience Measure and Structural Extreme Events Reconnaissance protocols. By combining rigorous statistical analysis with multidisciplinary fieldwork, Mayeux provides critical insights into both the social determinants of adolescent well-being and the engineering-societal factors governing disaster resilience.
